newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists, Communists map poll strategy.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists, Communists map poll strategy.

text.p: The heads of France's Socialist and Communist parties, uneasy allies when not outright enemies for nearly 80 years, tried on Tuesday to hammer out plans to beat the ruling centre-right coalition in a snap election.

Clearly expecting the talks to be difficult, both Socialist Lionel Jospin and Communist Robert Hue insisted they would aim solely to define goals rather than reach an official pact to govern together in case of victory in the May 25-June 1 poll.
But their meeting began under uncertain auspices after a first gathering of nearly all the left-wing groups earlier in the day attended by Socialists, Communists and smaller leftist movements.
That earlier meeting was to agree on single candidates for the first round of voting in constituencies where the extreme rightist National Front (FN) was expected to score heavily.
Participants said no agreement had been reached because the Communists told those present that they would not sign any agreement on the issue.

The more important Socialist-Communist policy meeting began several hours later in the heart of the Latin Quarter and was attended by heavyweights from both parties including Socialist former premier Laurent Fabius.

Jospin, whose party is forecast by most opinion polls to win about 220 seats compared with only 25 or so for the Communists in the 577-seat National Assembly, had levelled a warning to Hue even before they met.
"The Communist Party must ask itself questions about its historical future, about its identity and about its position," he told an election rally late on Monday.
"The Soviet Union has disappeared and the movement which began in 1917 ended the way we know in 1989. That means all those who were involved in that must ask themselves real questions," Jospin said.
His strong words were apparently aimed at countering warnings by centre-right politicians of the "Red menace" which a Socialist-Communist government might portend for France.
The French Communist Party was long one of the most staunchly pro-Soviet in Europe, run on strict Stalinist lines.
The well-informed daily newspaper Le Monde said on Tuesday that the document the two sides would sign made no mention of the Communists participating in a future cabinet.
Hue said on Monday that if the Communists participated in a cabinet, "it would show that the left has remained to the left".
The two parties differ on key issues including European unity and a single European currency, both of which the Communists oppose.
